As shown below, the file $f.c$ defines a function f whose code refers to the variable $x$ that is not a local variable or a parameter. The file $g.c$ defines a function $g$ whose code refers to the variable $x$ that is not a local variable or a parameter.

// file f.c
// declaration for x
void f(int a){
 ...
 x = ...
}
// file g.c
// declaration for x
void g(char* p){
 ...
 x = ...
}

The following table below shows how the variable x is defined in each file. For each row in the table, indicate in Column (c) whether the two functions at run-time refer to the SAME identifier (memory location) or to DIFFERENT identifiers (memory locations)
$$\begin{array} {|l|l|c|} \hline \qquad \textbf{Column A} & \qquad \textbf{Column B} & \textbf{Column C} \\ \textbf{declaration in f.c} & \textbf{declaration in g.c} & \textbf{SAME or DIFFERENT} \\\hline \text{int x;} & \text{extern int x;} & {\color{Red} {\textbf{SAME}}} \\\hline \text{int x = 0;} & \text{static int x;} & \\\hline \text{static int x;} & \text{static int x;} & \\\hline \text{static int x;} & \text{extern int x = 0;} & \\\hline \end{array}$$

The first row of column C has been filled for hints. What will be in the $2$nd, $3$rd, and $4$th row of Column C, respectively?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 32)

1.int x;

Is a global variable stored in static memory.

extern int x;

Is an indication of the presence of a global variable x either in the same or a linked file.

Since f.c has a declaration of x variable, g.c can access this x from f.c

Hence, both the files are referring to the same identifier.

2.int x=0;

Is a definition of a global variable stored in static memory.

static int x;

Is a static variable also stored in static memory. Although it is declared globally, static variables are not available to linker. They are available only to the functions of the same file. So, both the files are not referring to the same variable.

3.static int x;

Is a static variable declared globally stored in static memory.

static int x; of g.c

Is also stored in static memory, but both the variables are only available in their respective files.

So, they aren’t referring to the same variable.

4.static int x;

Is a static variable declared globally stored in static memory.

extern int x=0;

Which is extern int x;

int x=0;

Is referring to the global variable and is followed by its definition. Its different from the static variable in f.c

So, both the files aren’t referring to the same variable.

OPTION C- DIFFERENT, DIFFERENT, DIFFERENT

  • int x = 0; is defined globally and static int = 0; is also defined globally but not available to the linker.[DIFFERENT]

  • static int x; of both functions are defined globally but both the variables are available only to respective files.[DIFFERENT]

  • static int x; is defined globally with no linker but extern int x = 0; is basically extern int; int x = 0; having the functionality of linker. [DIFFERENT]

It is NOT referring to the static variable in f.c.

Different memory locations.

questions.qtext:
Consider the below program written into $2$ files.

Note that compilation of f$1$.c and f$2$.c happens independently of each other.

Which of the following is TRUE?

options.text: f$1$.c and f$2$.c can be compiled independently.
f$1$.c will produce a compilation error since variable $x$ does not get any memory, and we are using it in printf.
f$1$.c and f$2$.c can be compiled and linked. The output of the program will be $00.$
f$2$.c will produce a compilation error since function fun() is not defined in f$2$.c.

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 40)

Answer: A

A: Extern variable is just a declaration whose definition is looked for during linking phase. So compiling both files individually causes no issues.

B: This is true that x does not get any memory because this is just a declaration, however this will never cause compilation error. This may get linker error later on.

C: These can be compiled but can not be linked because in f2.c the definition of variable x is of type static, and static variables are not available to the linker. So the x which f1.c was looking for is never found.

D: Since the prototype of fun() is available with f2.c there will never be compilation error. Again there may be linker error later on if the definition is not found.

Source solution 2 (score: 5)
  • In f1.c: The declaration extern int x; states that the variable x is globally defined in another file. However, the compiler will look for the definition of x during the linking stage.
  • In f2.c: The declaration static int x; states that the variable x is defined as static, limiting its scope to f2.c. This means that the variable x even though defined globally within f2.c, cannot be accessed by other files (In this case f1.c). Because Static Storage Class limits its accessibility to the file/block it is declared in.
  • The function fun() is declared as void fun(); in f2.c but it is not defined within this file. The compiler treats it as an externally defined function, meaning its definition (implementation of the function) will be found in another file (In this case, f1.c).
  • Both f1.c and f2.c will compile independently without errors because the compiler only checks for syntax and semantics within each line. It doesn't check for cross-file dependencies during the compilation stage.
  • During the ​​​​linking stage, the linker attempts to resolve all the cross-file dependencies such as references to functions or variables declared as extern in one file and defined in another.
  • When the function fun() is called, the linker successfully resolves this reference because fun() is defined in f1.c.
  • Although the function fun() is correctly linked, the print() statement inside fun() requires the value of x, which is declared as extern in f1.c. Since x is declared as static in f2.c, it is not globally accessible. As a result, the linker cannot find a global definition of x , leading to a Linker error.
Source solution 3 (score: 0)

every variable and function used have their respective definations in their file therefore there is no problem in compilation. extern x tells the compiler that there might be a int variable x present in the file without any defination but dont throw an error as this defination might be present after the main or some other file . Same happens in f2.c where void fun(); is a declaration that fun might be present later or in some other file don't throw any compiler error .

But during linking phase as the only x defination prsesnt is in f2.c which is static therefore not availabe to the linker so extern can't point to that variable hence linking error.

One important variation could be that if in f2.c there is int x; instead of static int x; then there would be no linking error due to x. Functions which are not static in nature are also availabe to the linker therefore it will also not throw linker error hence both will be linked successfully .

questions.qtext: Which of the following(s) will evaluate to true
questions.solution:
Answer: C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 40)

Answer: C, D

Note that precedence and associativity tells us how the expression is parenthesized.
Then the expression is evaluated in the evaluation order in this case it is from left to right.

(A) Expression $0 \&\& 0==0$ is parenthesized as $0 \&\& (0==0)$ but when it is evaluated it is evaluated from left to right, since we get $0$ from the first expression due to short-circuiting in C we get $0$ and further evaluation will not take place.

Similarly in case of (B) we get 0.

(C) Expression $1 || 0==0$ is parenthesized as $1 || (0==0)$ but when it is evaluated it is evaluated from left to right, since we get $1$ from the first expression due to short-circuiting in C we get $1$ and further evaluation will not take place.

Similarly in case of (D) we get 1.

Now considering examples given by @shishir_roy,


$1||0,0$ is parenthesized as $(1||0),0$ and here short-circuiting will happen while calculating $(1||0)$ and $1$ will be returned. Now in case of comma operator rightmost expression value is returned so in our case $0$ will be returned hence we get $1||0,0=0$.

Similarly work it out for $0\&\&1, 1$.

Answer: Option C) & D)

questions.qtext:
What will be the output?

int a = 4, b =15, c =29;
if(c>b>a)
 printf("TRUE");
else
 printf("FALSE");
questions.solution:
Answer: C, B, A

Source solution 1 (score: 15)

Answer: B

Associativity of $>$ is from left to right, so $c>b>a$ will be evaluated as $(c>b)>a$. Since $c>b$ is true so expression will become $1>a$ which is false. Hence we will go to else statement and FALSE will be printed.

Source solution 2 (score: 6)

B is the answer.

Source solution 3 (score: 3)

The answer is B.

Same precedence but associativity is left to right.

29 > 15 is evaluated to 1 (Boolean True) in signed integer type and 1 > 4 is again signed comparison which would evaluate to 0 (Boolean False).

if(0) evaluates to FALSE hence,

else is executed and the final output is FALSE.

Source solution 4 (score: 0)

The correct option is B. FALSE.

🔑 The Core Concept: Left-to-Right Associativity

In C, relational operators like > have left-to-right associativity. This means that a chained expression like c > b > a does not evaluate as a mathematical range condition (like $c > b$ and $b > a$). Instead, the compiler evaluates it sequentially from left to right as (c > b) > a.

🔍 Step-by-Step Evaluation

Given variables: a = 4, b = 15, c = 29.

  1. Evaluate the first relational expression (c > b):
    • This simplifies to 29 > 15.
    • Since 29 is greater than 15, this expression evaluates to true, which in C is represented by the integer value 1.
  2. Substitute that result back into the main condition:
    • (c > b) > a
    • (1) > a
  3. Evaluate the final expression (1 > a):
    • This simplifies to 1 > 4.
    • Since 1 is not greater than 4, this expression evaluates to false, represented by the integer value 0.
  4. Execute the conditional blocks:
    • The if(0) condition fails, skipping the printf("TRUE"); block.
    • The execution falls through to the else block, triggering printf("FALSE");.

🔑 The Core Concept: Lvalues and Rvalues

In C, the single equals sign (=) is the assignment operator. It requires two components:

  • Left-Hand Side (LHS): Must be a modifiable lvalue (a locator value that refers to a specific memory location where data can be stored, such as a variable name like x).
  • Right-Hand Side (RHS): Can be any rvalue (a temporary value or expression that evaluates to a number, such as y + z).
❌ Option A: x + 5 = y + z (Invalid)
  • The LHS is x + 5. This is a mathematical expression that evaluates to a temporary rvalue, not a modifiable memory location.
  • You cannot assign a value to a temporary mathematical expression. Compiling this will throw a lvalue required as left operand of assignment compilation error.
Option B: x = y = z + w (Valid)
  • The assignment operator has right-to-left associativity.
  • This expression safely evaluates as x = (y = (z + w)). The sum z + w is assigned to variable y, and that resulting value is then assigned to variable x.
Option C: x = (z - y) == w (Valid)
  • The equality operator (==) has a higher precedence than the assignment operator (=).
  • The compiler evaluates whether (z - y) is equal to w. This comparison results in either 1 (true) or 0 (false), which is then perfectly valid to store inside the variable x.
Option D: w = x != y && z (Valid)
  • Operator precedence orders this expression as: w = ((x != y) && z).
  • It first checks if x is not equal to y, performs a logical AND with z, and assigns the final true/false result (1 or 0) to w.

questions.qtext:
What will be the output of the following C program?.
Here $?:$ is a ternary operator which is right to left-associative.

#include <stdio.h>
int main() {
 int i =2, j =1;
 if (--j ? ++j? i : i++ : i--)
 printf("%d%d\n", i, j);
}
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 12)

Answer : A. 1 0

Initially i = 2 and j = 1.

Condition -> --j ? ++j ? i : i++ : i-- which is equivalent

to -> --j ? [ ++j ? i : i++ ] : i--

First --j is evaluated which makes j = 0 and returns 0 (false); therefore the condition is false so i-- is evaluated next which returns 2 (true) and makes i = 1

So we print (i,j) -> 1 0

Source solution 2 (score: 12)

One of the easy method to solve these types of questions is to convert ternary into if-else .

if( --j ? ++j ? i : i++ : i--);

This statement can be rewritten as :

if (--j)
{ 
 if(++j)
 {
 i;
 }
 else {
 i++;
 }
}
else {
 i--;
}

Now if you dry run this code you will get i=1 , j=0

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

Common Misconception! Placing an expression inside an if condition does not protect variables from being changed.

NOTE: Any side-effects like modifications, increments (++), or decrements (--) will definitely modify the variables in memory as long as that specific part of the code gets evaluated.

The conditional operator (? :) has right-to-left associativity. The nested expression inside the if statement is parsed by the compiler like this:

$$\text{- -j } ? \ (\text{++j } ? \ \text{i} : \text{i++}) : \text{i- -}$$

Initially, the variables are: i = 2, j = 1.

Step A: Evaluate the main condition (--j)

  • --j is a pre-decrement operator.
  • It modifies j in memory immediately: j drops from 1 to 0.
  • The value returned by this expression is the new value, which is 0 (False).

Step B: Follow the conditional branches (Short-Circuiting)

  • Because the condition evaluated to 0 (False), the compiler completely skips the true branch: (++j ? i : i++).
  • This means ++j and i++ are never executed, so j remains 0.
  • The execution jumps directly to the false branch: i--.

Step C: Evaluate the false branch (i--)

  • i-- is a post-decrement operator.
  • The expression returns the current value of i first, which is 2.
  • Right after returning that value, it decrements i in memory: i drops from 2 to 1.

🖨️ 3. Final Output Evaluation

  • The final value returned to the if condition from the entire expression is 2.
  • Since 2 is a non-zero value, the if statement treats it as TRUE.
  • Because it is true, the program proceeds to run the inner statement: printf("%d%d\n", i, j);.

Printing the current values in memory:

  • i is now 1
  • j is now 0

Output: 1 0

Source solution 4 (score: 0)

Answer : A

  1. For the ternary operator ( ? : ) the associativity is fixed from R -> L, and it's order of evaluation is also fixed from L -> R just like Logical AND ( && ), Logical OR ( || ), etc.
  2. Hence associativity groups the expression like this :
    --j ? ( ++j ? i : i++ ) : i--
  3. But the evaluation happens from L -> R, hence "--j" is evaluated first and based on the result of it "i--" is evaluated next.

questions.qtext:
Professor Greg wants to give assignments to his students to write a $C$ program for the $\text{XOR5}$ function. $\text{XOR5}$ is a function that returns true if and only if $\text{EXACTLY}$ one of the integers $A$ and $B$ is $5$.
Using which of the following condition(s), $\text{XOR5}$ can be implemented?
questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C, D

Selected solution (score: 31)
We can also solve this question using concepts from propositional logic.

The logic underlying the == operator is the biconditional logical operator($\Leftrightarrow$).
So, the != operator will be the negation of biconditional logical operator which is the xor logical operator($\oplus$).

Now, let $A==5$ be the proposition $P$ and $B==5$ be the proposition $Q$.

$XOR5$ is the proposition $P \oplus Q$.

$\textbf{A.}$ $P != Q$ $\equiv P \oplus Q$.

$\therefore$ $A.$ is correct.

$\textbf{B.}$ $!P != !Q$ $\equiv \neg P \oplus \neg Q \equiv P \oplus Q$.

$\therefore$ $B.$ is correct.

$\textbf{C.}$ $(P\ ?\ !Q : \ Q)$ $\equiv (P \Rightarrow \neg Q)\land(\neg P \Rightarrow Q) \equiv (\neg P \lor \neg Q)\land(P \lor Q) \equiv P \oplus Q$.

$\therefore$ $C.$ is correct.

$\textbf{D.}$ $(P \lor Q) \land \neg(P \land Q) \equiv (P \lor Q) \land (\neg P \lor \neg Q)$ $\equiv P \oplus Q$.

$\therefore$ $D.$ is correct.
Source solution 2 (score: 17)

Correct answer: A, B, C, D

Let’s see options one by one,

  1. $(A==5)!=(B==5)$ will return true only when one of the condition is true, if both are true and both are false it will return false. Hence this is a right option.
  2. It can also be seen as $(A!=5)!=(B!=5)$ it will return true when one of the condition is false, if both are false and both are true it will return false just as in option A. Hence this is also right option.
  3. Consider when $A==5$ it will return $!(B==5)$ if B is also 5 then it will return false else it will return true. Now if $A !=5$ it will return $(B==5)$ which only returns true when $B==5$. This is also a correct option.
  4. $((A==5)||(B==5))$ returns true if either one or both are equal to 5 but $!((A==5) \;\&\&\; (B==5))$ returns false when both are equal to 5, and we know $T \land F = F$. So this is also correct option.

questions.qtext:
Let the variables $x,y,$ and $z$, be of type int and assigned some values. The variable $b1$ is initialized as follows:

int b1 = (x > z) && (y >= z);

Variables b2, b3, b4, and b5 are initialized below.

int b2 = (x <= z) || (y < z) 
int b3 = !((x < z) || (y <= z)) 
int b4 = !((x < z) && (y >= z)) 
int b5 = ((x > z) && (y > z)) || ((x > z) && (y == z))

Variables $b2, b3, b4$, and $b5$ ALWAYS, SOMETIMES, or NEVER takes the same value as $b1$.
Which of the variable(s) SOMETIMES takes the same value as $b1$?
questions.solution:
Answer: B, C

Selected solution (score: 39)

Let $P(a,b)$ be the predicate $a > b$ and $Q(a,b)$ be the predicate $a \ge b$.

$\neg P(a,b)$ is $a \le b$ and $\neg Q(a,b)$ is $a < b$.

We can rewrite $b1$, $b2$,…, $b5$ in terms of these predicates using propositional logic symbols.

The question asks whether $b1 \Leftrightarrow bi$ is Valid, Contingency or a Contradiction.

$b1 \equiv P(x,z) \land Q(y, z)$

$b2 \equiv \neg P(x,z) \lor \neg Q(y,z) \equiv \neg b1$.

$b1 \Leftrightarrow b2$ is a Contradiction.

So, $b2$ NEVER takes the same value as $b1$.

$b3 \equiv \neg(\neg Q(x,z) \lor \neg P(y,z)) \equiv P(y,z) \land Q(x,z)$

Clearly this is not the same expression as $b1$ but it sometimes takes the same value as $b1$ (eg. when $x = y$).

$b1 \Leftrightarrow b3$ is a Contingency.

So, $b3$ SOMETIMES takes the same value as $b1$.

$b4 \equiv \neg(\neg Q(x,z) \land Q(y,z)) \equiv Q(x,z) \lor \neg Q(y,z)$

If $x > z$ and $y >= z$ then $b1$ and $b4$ both are true.
If $x=z$ then $b4$ is true but $b1$ is false.

$b1 \Leftrightarrow b4$ is a Contingency.

So, $b4$ SOMETIMES takes the same value as $b1$.

$
\begin{align*}
b5 &\equiv [P(x,z) \land P(y,z)] \lor [P(x,z) \land (\ Q(y,z) \land \neg P(y,z)\ )] \\
&\equiv P(x,z) \land[P(y,z) \lor (\ Q(y,z) \land \neg P(y,z)\ )] &\text{[Distributive property]} \\
&\equiv P(x,z) \land [\ \underbrace{\underbrace{P(y,z)}_{\Large y\ >\ z} \lor \underbrace{Q(y,z)}_{\Large y\ \ge\ z}}_{\Large y\ \ge\ z \ =\ Q(y,\ z)}\ ] &[\because A \lor (\neg A \land B) \equiv A \lor B] \\
b5 &\equiv P(x,z) \land Q(y,z) \equiv b1 \\
\end{align*}
$

$b1 \Leftrightarrow b5$ is Valid.

So, $b5$ ALWAYS takes the same value as $b1$.

$\bf \therefore \text{Ans: B, C}$

Consider the following two .$c$ files which both include the same $.h$ file:


When compiled, linked, and executed, the following output results:
$x = 1 \; y = 2\; z = 3\; w = 4\; v = 5$
Assuming that this program compiled and linked successfully, and based on the output shown above, add static and/or extern modifiers to the blank lines $(1)$ through $(10)$.

Leave them blank if neither modifier would be appropriate.

For example, if we say line $(2)$ is static then we consider line $(2)$ as $\text{“static int x”}$. Or if we say line $(9)$ is empty then we treat line $9$ as $\text{“int w = 4”}$.

options.text:
Line$(1)$ – empty
Line$(2)$ - static

Line$(4)$ - extern
Line$(5)$ – empty
Line$(6)$ - empty

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Selected solution (score: 14)

(1) Needs to be static, or else linking fails due to 2 conflicting strong symbols ‘inc’ with an “already defined” error

(2) x must be static. If it weren’t, and a.c and b.c shared the same x, its value would be 2, not 1.

(3) y should be extern (it must be shared between a.c and b.c, else its value wouldn’t be 2.) However, leaving it without modifier works also (For what its worth, int y; followed by int y = 1; compiles and the strong definition is used.) It cannot be static.

(4) z’s modifier must be blank so that ‘z’ becomes a common symbol (shared, but weak). If extern were used, z would be nowhere defined (undefined reference error). If static were used, it would have the value 4, not 3. Note that defining ‘z’ in a header file is generally considered bad practice.

(5) Should be extern (or left blank, which has identical semantics for functions.) If it were static, ‘b’ would be undefined in a.c

(6) Must be blank – static would conflict with the earlier declaration of y in the header file. Extern, which declares a variable, is incompatible with an initialization, which can only be used with a definition.

(7) Like (3), can be extern or blank. Note that neither choice is good design. If extern, the declaration should appear in a header. If blank, the definition is redundant (and will be dominated by b.c’s strong definition of w.

(8) Must be static since the value printed is 5 – a.c has its own copy of ‘v’

(9) Must be blank so that ‘w’ is defined globally. If static, a.o would have an resolved reference. Like (6), you cannot use extern with a definition.

(10) Could be blank or static. b.c could operate on a global symbol for ‘v’, or have a local copy – either way, it will not affect the output. Like (9), it cannot be extern.

Source solution 2 (score: 12)

The preprocessor generates a modified version of the source code, which includes the content of the header files and the values of the macros. This happens prior to compilation.

In the given source code, after the preprocessing stage, the contents of “a.h” will be available to both “a.c” and “b.c”.

Line (1): ___ int inc (int x) { .. };
This has to be Static. Since this is inside header file, it will be copied into the modified source code, before compilation. So there will be two copies of the same function, one in each file.
If we have it Empty or Extern, then during the linking process, Linker will not be able to distinguish the two functions and it will result in ambiguity / name conflict.
So, if we have it as static, then we are making sure this function is not visible for linking.

Line (2): ___ int x;
This cannot be extern because there is no other definition anywhere.
This may be Static or Global. During execution, the value of x remains unaffected, this is because both “a.c” and “b.c” will be working with its own version of “a.h”.

Line (3): ___ int y;
In “a.c”, y is declared globally in Line (6) and assigned a value 1. So, line (3) has to be extern to avoid conflicts.
During execution, the value of y changes from 1 to 2, this happens because call to b() increments y. From “b.c” point of view, y is declared as extern, which refers to the definition at Line(6) in “a.c”.

Line (4): ___ int z;
This cannot be extern because there is no other definition anywhere.
This cannot be static, because we know static variables are not available for linking. But here, we see the value of z is made 4 by “a.c” and next it is decremented by “b.c”, and final result is 3. For this to happen, z must be global (empty).

Line (5): ___ void b(void);
Function void b(void) is being used externally inside of “a.c” while it’s definition is in “b.c”. For the declaration, we may have it as Extern or Empty.

Line (6): ___ int y = 1;
This has to be Global (empty), since Line (3) is extern.

Line (7): ___ int w;
The value of w is defined in “b.c” even though it is being used in “a.c”. So, it has to be declared as extern.

Line (8): ___ int v=5;
The variable v in “a.c” is initialized to 5, and is not affected by b(). So it must be declared as Static.

Line (9): ___ int w=4;
The variable w is being initialized here, which is being referred externally by “a.c”. So it must be global (empty).

Line (10): ___ int v=5;
The variable v in “b.c” is independent of v in “a.c”. So it may be declared as Static or Global.

Answer: B

Source solution 3 (score: 7)

Answer : B
1. static - function definition, cannot be left empty or made extern, so as to avoid name conflict.
2. static - from the result we can conclude both x's are different in file a.c and b.c
3. extern - since y is defined in file a.c and is being used by function in file b.c (from output we can conclude it)
4. empty - it can’t be made extern since there’s no other definition of z and will cause undefined reference error. it can’t be made static also since it is being used in file b.c (from output we can conclude it)
5. extern/empty - function declaration
6. extern/empty - must not be made static since y is being used by another file b.c
7. extern - since w is defined in file b.c
8. static - since this v is not same as that of file b.c
9. extern/empty - must not be made static since w is being used by another file a.c
10. static - since this v is not same as that of file a.c

In 6 and 9, we can also use extern because when used with definitions extern also creates memory for that variable, but compiler will give warning.

Answer :- B

questions.qtext:
Consider the following variable and function definitions:

int g=10;
int q3() {
 static int g=5;
 return ++g;
}
int q4() {
 extern int g;
 return ++g;
}
int q5() {
 int g=1;
 return ++g;
}

What is the value of the expression $q3() + q3() + q4() + q4() + q5() + q5()?$
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 16)

Answer: 40

Points to note/remember:

  1. Static variables are stored in static memory and hence even if activation record of a function is popped the value of static variable persists Global variables are also stored in static memory.
  2. Although associativity of addition operator is defined (L>R) and
q3()+q3()+q4()+q4()+q5()+q5()

will be interpreted as

((((q3() + q3()) + q4()) + q4()) + q5()) + q5()

the final addition can only be done after the values are returned, but the order in which the following functions are evaluated is not defined. So in (q3() + q4()) for example we can say for sure which among q3 and q4 which one is evaluated first. This could be concerning because of static variable since value of variable persists between function calls and it may lead to race condition (final result depends on order of evaluation). This however is not concerning in this question as we’re just adding the result and addition is commutative but if this were subtraction then the result may not be consistent among different compilers.

  1. Extern int g in function q4 refers to global int g.

So,

q3 runs and initialize it’s local static int g to 5, make it 6 and returns (pre increment), now again when q3 runs, read the static value (static variables are initialized only once) as 6, make it 7 and returns.

q4 runs and does basically same but with global variable and 11 and 12.

q5 runs and initialize local int var g to 1 and make it 2 and returns. But since the variable was not static it was stored in the activation record of q5, which (AR) was destroyed/popped right when q5 returned. Now when q5 runs again repeats itself, initialize, add, returns 2.

Hence the expression

q3()+q3()+q4()+q4()+q5()+q5()

becomes 6 + 7 + 11 + 12 + 2 + 2 = 40

Source solution 2 (score: 10)

ANSWER : 40

Expression to evaluate : q3() + q3() + q4() + q4() + q5() + q5()

given, global int g = 10

now when q3() is called,

static int g = 5 is defined, and return ++g will return 6 and increment static variable g of q3 to 6.

so now our expression is : 6 + q3() + q4() + q4() + q5() + q5()



again, q3() is called,

now since g inside of q3 is static it won’t be initialized again, therefore return ++g will return 7 and increment g of q3 to 7

so now our expression is : 6 + 7 + q4() + q4() + q5() + q5()


now q4 is called,

it has extern int g which will refer to global g which has value 10, return ++g will return 11 and increment global g to 11.

so now our expression is : 6 + 7 + 11 + q4() + q5() + q5()

and global g = 11



again q4 is called, and return ++g will return 12 and increment global g to 12.

so now our expression is : 6 + 7 + 11 + 12 + q5() + q5()

and global g = 12



now q5 is called,

it has local g = 1, return ++g will return 2 and increment g to 2 but it will be destroyed as end of function is reached.

so now our expression is : 6 + 7 + 11 + 12 + 2 + q5()



again q5 is called,

again g = 1 will be initialized as it is local variable and ++g will return 2 and g becomes 2 and get destroyed.

so now our expression is : 6 + 7 + 11 + 12 + 2 + 2


therefore, our expression becomes : 6 + 7 + 11 + 12 + 2 + 2 = 40 ( ANSWER)


NOTE : the order in which functions are called here does not matter, the answer remains same.

Source solution 3 (score: 1)

q3( ) :

static int g = 5 // This will create it’s own local static copy of g

return ++g // Uses it’s own static local copy. So, first the value will be incremented and then returned i.e = 6

q3( ) :

static int g = 5 // This doesn’t gets executed as static variables are executed only once.

return ++g // It uses the local copy of g which was executed in the first call i.e = 7

q4( ) :

extern int g; // It simply references to a global variable created at the beginning of program.

return ++g; // The global g is accessed and pre incremented i.e = 11

q4( ) :

extern int g; // Again it simply references to a global variable created at the beginning of program.

return ++g; // The global g is accessed and pre incremented i.e = 12

q5( ) :

int g = 1; // It creates its own local copy the value of g is initialized to 1. So, here g = 1

return ++g; // It uses the local copy of g and returns pre incremented value i.e = 2

q5( ) :

int g = 1; // Again it creates its own local copy the value of g is again initialized to 1. So, here again g = 1

return ++g; // It uses the local copy of g and returns pre incremented value i.e = 2

q3()+q3()+q4()+q4()+q5()+q5() = 6 + 7 + 11 + 12 + 2 + 2 = 40 (Ans)
